So I've been trying to find no knead breads to enjoy recently, just to have something to go with my soups for winter. So after much trial and error, this one I have found produces the best results thus far.

I did fuck up, and instead of leaving it for 12 hours to rise, I left it for about 20 because I had to go out, but even then, it still came out quite well... well enough to go with a nice stew I had made. However when I left it for its second rise of 2 hours, it didn't double in size, making it a bit more dense than I was expecting. I'll try different methods and times in the future.

Over all, it came out like a really light sour dough. I expect if I time it properly next time and rise it better so it actually doubles, I'll have a less dense loaf. Also, a Pyrex container works excellently here if you don't have any cast iron pots with lids. Even a lined bread tin with al-foil over the top will be good (but not preferable, as it needs to be pre heated and hold heat to cook the underside nice and crisp).
How warm is it where you live? I live in a cold place and I almost always end up waiting longer than 12/2 hours for both rises. If it hasn't doubled after 2 hours, I would wait some more.

Well, its the day after the winter solstice here and I'm sitting with a window open and wearing long pants and a cotton shirt. It does get 'cold' here, but I left it to rise in a heated room at about 24C. I think I will leave it longer just in case, but I did think my initial 20 hour instead of 12 hour initial rise may have affected it. I will be trying again tomorrow for my tomato and chicken soup.

Its much quicker to make bread in summer, but a pain in the ass to make other things like pavlova, puff pastry or eclairs.

Originally posted on /r/techno_commercialism

There are two interrelated reasons why cartels implode. It is in the self interest of each member to defect, to their net detriment. And there is no way to enforce the agreement to deter defection.

The traditional way to work around this is to lobby the state to enforce the cartel's policies. A historical example is the formation of IG Farben. The German chemical industry had an oligopolistic structure, with the major players being BASF, Bayer, and Hoechst. They formed cartels, and they were imperfect. To reliably enforce cartel pricing, the three merged with the support of the German state to form a monopoly that lasted until their benefactor state itself collapsed from war.

I propose that cartels can transcend the self interest of members in a different way than monopolizing under state protection. They can use a distributed system of validating compliance to the pact, similar to how any other agreed upon rule is self-enforcing on a blockchain like consensus network.

For a simpler example: BASF, Bayer, and Hoechst could get together and decide they could maximize summed income from bromine with a price of $10 per pound. To prevent defection, the validity of their offers depends on the compliance of the offers of the others. Defection can be known to cause an immediate price war down to a level which lowers the income of the single firm from what it could have been. 'Tit for tat' strategy becomes an algorithmic certainty, strongly deterring defection. This would be a crypto cartel that enforces its policies through incentive.

A second way to enforce a crypto cartel would be through cryptography itself. Each of the firms generates a key pair. They each sign and release a message which says to only consider transactions valid if they are also signed by the other two members of the cartel - this is using multisig transactions. This mechanism of enforcement means that defection using the company keys is cryptographically impossible. But that doesn't stop them from simply creating a new key pair and leaving.

A crypto cartel would likely use some combination of these mechanisms. They would rely on multisig transactions to validate actions against predefined cartel policy, and they would use smart contacts set for tit-for-tat to disincentivize leaving the group.
What prevents Unilever from entering the Bromine market and undercutting the cartel?

Nothing. It does provide an incentive for them to want to be brought into the fold, to join the self-enforcing cartel. And them undercutting provides the cartel members an incentive to want to bring them in too.

The bigger issue that this in no way prevents is innovative disruption. The cartel can be made reasonably stable, but the reliance on a given method of production or even the product itself cannot.

It's an interesting way to bring cartels in the crypto age. While it's certainly possible to perform transactions the way you describe... why go through the trouble? I think it would be easier post today's agreed to price + today's date and have every cartel member sign it with their private key.

I don't see how cryptography changes cartel incentives. If a cartel member wants to defect and sell at a lower price I don't see anything stopping them, simply don't use the agreed upon crypto infrastructure which is exactly what a new entrant who wants to break up a cartel would do.

Tools

Can you explain something to me? I was reading about electrum and armory and I noticed in some screenshots the option "send bitcoins". You mentioned about using bitcoin on an offline machine. How does one send/receive bitcoins without an internet connection?

Not OP but I will give a quick answer.

A bitcoin address is generated using entropy, no internet connection is required for that part. So you can make an address offline and send the public address over to a live machine for receiving while leaving the private key offline.

Basically to send bitcoin to another address a signed transaction has to happen, the private key is what signs the transaction. You would use a live machine to generate a transaction and then move it over to a secure offline environment to be signed by the private key, you then move the signed transaction back over to the live machine to be broadcast. This is obviously a hassle for some but the most secure way to deal with bitcoin.

My post above highlights some easier ways - https://voat.co/v/bitcoin/comments/161916/430291

Receiving is easy. All you need is a public address and the corresponding private key. You share the public key to get paid.

Spending requires the private key. Private keys are secret. You can "sweep" a private key to a public key bitcoin address, thereby spending ALL the bitcoin held. You can also sign a transaction for any amount of the bitcoin held in the bitcoin address.

It's much easier to receive bitcoin to cold storage than it is to spend bitcoin bitcoin from cold storage. This is the nature of cold storage. Cold storage requires total security of the private key(s).

Electrum and Armory are hybrid cold and hot wallet solutions that facilitate sending and receiving bitcoin.

I recommend a two or three pronged approach. Have a hot wallet that you regularly spend from and replenish to. Have a cold wallet that requires less frequent spending. Have a super cold wallet that you only add to.

Get a bitcoin wallet that works with your device. Your level of risk aversion will determine your wallet choice.

If privacy is a concern, there are three primary objectives.

  1. Obscure your obtaining bitcoin. BitQuick.co or LocalBitcoins are your best bets. If you are new to bitcoin, BitQuick is more user friendly. I was able to get $50 worth of bitcoin in under 3 hours with paper money and no car.

  2. Obscure receiving the bitcoin. This is more difficult. You will need a wallet address that is not linked to your IP. I'm not going into these details here. The easiest way, if you aren't totally privacy paranoid, is to just download Mycelium on your mobile device. This will also simplify spending your bitcoin. Offline cold storage receiving is best for privacy.

  3. Obscure spending your bitcoin. Spending is only as obscure the sum of the privacy risk assumed from receiving bitcoin + risk from spending. If you order a physical item to your house with bitcoin, obscurity is limited only to those that have both your spending bitcoin address or your physical address. The same applies to any IP address associated with your spending.

Privacy on the internet is fairly impossible for all but the most paranoid privacy practitioners. Bitcoin is no exception. The weakest link will break.

Security is much easier. Read bitcoin security basics, and I will be happy to answer any questions about bitcoin security.

It all depends on your own security level of course. It also depends if you're going to store 0,001 BTC in your wallet or 5 BTC.

If you're an IT professional maybe you can get away with using a Windows or Mac client and just storing your bitcoin there. I would say you're taking a risk though because there's no protection at all if someone steals your private key. Maybe then I would recommend storing a small amount of BTC for everyday use in your hot online wallet and larger amounts in cold storage so it can't be stolen online.

If you're an average user maybe it's best to use a mobile device, because it's much harder to crack a mobile device if it's not jailbroken. I also feel it's very important to keep things simple. An average user should only need to know how to install the mobile wallet, his own bitcoin address and how to make a backup of the wallet in case the mobile device gets stolen or stops working.
